title: Release-train pin semantics: channel/tag, semver ranges, and commit-hash binding with performance-profile snapshot
creator: Riley Patel
description:
Problem: Customers pin models in many ways today (friendly tags like 'stable', semver ranges, and opaque commit hashes). The runtime and SDK currently have underspecified precedence rules and no first-class binding between a pin and the performance profile used to compile/benchmark that pinned model. This creates risks: silent quality regressions when a tag moves, caching anomalies when different model binaries share an alias, and operational confusion during rollbacks.

Proposal summary: Introduce a deterministic, ordered pin-resolution contract exposed in the API and SDKs and add an immutable performance-profile snapshot reference to every pin. Pins will be represented as an immutable binding object: {pin_type, selector, resolved_ref, profile_snapshot_id, resolved_at, provenance}. Resolution precedence will be: 1) exact commit hash (sha-like) 2) explicit semver exact (1.2.3) 3) semver range (>=1.2.0 <2.0.0) with highest matching semver preferred 4) release channel tag (stable, beta) 5) floating alias (latest) fallback. The SDK will expose a PinResolutionResult with fields for resolved_ref and profile_snapshot_id and a small set of warnings when resolution was fuzzy (e.g., range matched multiple candidates).

Key design decisions: 
- Immutable pin objects: once a pin resolves to a resolved_ref + profile_snapshot_id, the runtime stores that binding in the pin cache and uses the snapshot id to select kernels/quantization parameters. This avoids hidden regressions if a tag moves later.
- Profile snapshot binding: performance profiles (latency/cost/kv-cache-optimizations/quantization) are saved as versioned snapshots. A pin will always reference a profile snapshot id that was generated for the resolved model binary. If a model author uploads a new binary, a new snapshot id is created; old pins continue to reference the older snapshot.
- Precedence and deterministic tiebreaking: semver ranges pick the highest semver satisfying the range. Tags are last-resort; floating aliases like 'latest' are explicitly discouraged for production pins and will generate high-severity warnings in SDKs.
- Environment overrides and scope: pins can be scoped by environment (hosted/dedicated/private) and by deployment scope (project or org). The resolution algorithm accepts an optional scope parameter; if not provided, the default project scope is used.
- TTL for fuzzy pins: for non-exact selectors (tags or ranges), the system will assign a stability window for caching the resolution (default 24h). During that window, subsequent resolutions return the cached binding. After the window expires, resolution is re-evaluated to pick newer binaries if available. Exact commit-pin bypasses TTL and is stable forever.
- Rollback semantics: when rolling back, clients should pin to the previous exact commit-hash or profile_snapshot_id. The console will expose a 'revert to binding' action that pins to the exact resolved_ref+profile_snapshot_id from a prior rollout.

Compatibility and migration: 
- Older clients that send only a string selector remain supported. Runtime will attempt to detect format (hash vs semver vs tag) and apply precedence, but servers will include resolution metadata in responses. SDKs will be updated to parse server metadata and surface it. We will add deprecation warnings for using unscoped floating aliases in production.

Observability: Every resolution will emit a structured event: selector, resolved_ref, profile_snapshot_id, resolve_path (exact|semver_range|tag|alias), resolution_latency_ms, cache_hit boolean. Console dashboards will include a pin-resolution heatmap and a list of pins referencing a profile snapshot for easier impact analysis.
acceptance_criteria: API returns PinResolutionResult containing resolved_ref and profile_snapshot_id for every model selection request
Runtime stores immutable binding for exact pins and caches fuzzy pins for TTL with appropriate expiry
SDK surface exposes a PinResolutionResult object and warns when a floating alias is used in production code paths
Performance profile snapshots are versioned and immutable; pins reference snapshot ids and runtime uses them to pick kernels/quant configs
Console shows history of resolved bindings and allows 'revert to binding' to pin previous resolved_ref+snapshot_id
updates: 2026-02-20: Kickoff sync with runtime, SDK, and console leads. Agreed precedence list and profile snapshot binding concept.
2026-02-25: Implemented initial API shape for PinResolutionResult; prototyped server-side binding cache with TTL.
2026-03-03: Spike showed that existing profiling pipeline needs a small extension to emit snapshot ids during profile generation; engineering will add snapshot metadata to publish job.
2026-03-10: Security reviewed scope/metadata and confirmed no secrets leak via resolution events; added privacy guard for customer edge-case names.
Next: SDK changes (JS/Python), runtime binding enforcement, and console UI for revert + audit log.
testing_plan: Unit tests for pin resolution precedence with exhaustive selector permutations (hash, semver exact, semver range, tag, alias)
Contract tests between SDK and server: SDK asserts presence of profile_snapshot_id and emits warning hooks for floating aliases
Integration tests: publish a sequence of model binaries and profiles, assert cached fuzzy pin behavior and TTL expiry
Canary e2e: staged rollout across 3 customers with telemetry to monitor latency, cost-per-token delta, and quality regressions tied to profile_snapshot_id
Chaos test: move a tag during the stability window and assert cached bindings do not silently flip until TTL expiry
rollout_plan: Stage 1 (safe): API + server-side binding cache behind feature flag; run on internal staging infra; collect resolution telemetry for 48h
Stage 2 (canary): Enable feature flag for 5% of hosted traffic and two Dedicated customers with opt-in; add SDK opt-in warnings
Stage 3 (wider): Release SDK updates; enable in console UI (pin history + revert) and flip feature flag for 50% traffic; monitor dashboards for regressions
Stage 4 (GA): Remove feature flag after 2 weeks without regressions; announce deprecation of floating alias usage in production; update docs and quickstart
